entries.title: Linking Women’s Equality With Government Integrity: Can Gender Budgeting Curb Corruption?
entries.abstract: ABSTRACT Policies addressing gender inequality have increasingly been linked to more ethical governance, as women tend to be disproportionately burdened by corruption compared to men. One such policy is gender budgeting, an innovative approach to resource allocation that considers the impact of government spending on women and other underrepresented groups. Despite the growing popularity worldwide, we know little about its effectiveness in curbing corruption. This study evaluates the impact of gender budgeting on grand (political) and petty (bureaucratic) corruption using difference‐in‐differences estimations across a panel of 136 countries from 1980 to 2023. The results reveal a significant reduction in petty corruption, as gender budgeting improves the impartiality of public bureaucracies. entries.title: How municipalities organise policy implementation under weak enforcement
entries.abstract: Municipalities in Spain are subject to legal transparency requirements that are weakly enforced. This article examines how municipalities organise implementation under weak enforcement: how arrangements change over time, who takes responsibility and what prompts them to change. Drawing on 51 interviews with officers in charge of transparency in municipalities of varying sizes and compliance levels, we trace how implementation has evolved since 2010. We find that municipalities typically assign transparency duties to existing staff and structures, rather than creating dedicated roles. Although legal enactment often initiates implementation, moves towards more specialised arrangements are associated with external incentives, such as evaluations or rankings, rather than with legal enactment alone. entries.title: Corruption Perceptions, the Pendleton Act, and Sovereign Borrowing Costs
entries.abstract: ABSTRACT Significant research suggests that systems of bureaucratic patronage tend to promote corruption and reduce the efficient production of publicly provided goods. However, much less work has been done to consider how market actors perceive such selection processes and especially reforms implemented to reduce such corruption. This study rectifies this by evaluating how the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act impacted federal borrowing costs. If patronage resulted in increased corruption and bureaucratic inefficiency, this should be reflected in relatively higher bond yields. If the Pendleton Act was successful in curbing this behavior, then this should be rewarded by market actors in the form of lower borrowing costs. entries.title: Excessive Heat and Correctional Officer Turnover: Evidence From Texas
entries.abstract: ABSTRACT Correctional work is difficult, dangerous, and hot. Many US prisons lack air‐conditioning, resulting in sweltering conditions for both incarcerated people and the street‐level bureaucrats tasked with their supervision. We examine the effect of working in the summer heat without air‐conditioning on correctional officer turnover using personnel records of nearly 60,000 Texas Department of Criminal Justice (TDCJ) employees across 68 prisons between 2010 and 2023. We demonstrate that, among the least‐experienced frontline employees before the onset of COVID‐19, the difference in the probability of departing between those working in prisons without and with air‐conditioning is, on average, 0.33 percentage points larger in the hottest months than in the coolest—an approximately 12% change relative to the baseline departure rate. entries.title: Elections, Expert Assessments and Public Sector Leaks: Evidence From a Survey Experiment
entries.abstract: ABSTRACT Despite strong normative, professional and legal constraints, leaks of confidential information by public administrators continue to arise. Yet, data limitations restrict our knowledge about when such actions are most/least likely. Conceptualizing the decision to leak confidential information as a “bureaucratic dilemma,” we theorize that this decision is affected by election proximity and positive/negative expert assessments of policy proposals. We test the resulting theoretical propositions via a between‐subjects survey experiment among 1661 national public administrators in Norway. Our results reveal that impending elections reduce the perceived probability of leaks among public administrators who support government parties, while having the reverse effect among public administrators not supporting government parties. entries.title: Elections, Expert Assessments and Public Sector Leaks: Evidence From a Survey Experiment
entries.abstract: ABSTRACT Despite strong normative, professional and legal constraints, leaks of confidential information by public administrators continue to arise. Yet, data limitations restrict our knowledge about when such actions are most/least likely. Conceptualizing the decision to leak confidential information as a “bureaucratic dilemma,” we theorize that this decision is affected by election proximity and positive/negative expert assessments of policy proposals. We test the resulting theoretical propositions via a between‐subjects survey experiment among 1661 national public administrators in Norway. Our results reveal that impending elections reduce the perceived probability of leaks among public administrators who support government parties, while having the reverse effect among public administrators not supporting government parties. entries.title: How municipalities organise policy implementation under weak enforcement
entries.abstract: Municipalities in Spain are subject to legal transparency requirements that are weakly enforced. This article examines how municipalities organise implementation under weak enforcement: how arrangements change over time, who takes responsibility and what prompts them to change. Drawing on 51 interviews with officers in charge of transparency in municipalities of varying sizes and compliance levels, we trace how implementation has evolved since 2010. We find that municipalities typically assign transparency duties to existing staff and structures, rather than creating dedicated roles. Although legal enactment often initiates implementation, moves towards more specialised arrangements are associated with external incentives, such as evaluations or rankings, rather than with legal enactment alone. entries.title: Interpersonal trust in the policy advisory process: a research agenda
entries.abstract: Interpersonal trust is a key factor determining whether advice is taken into account in policy making, yet it has received little substantive attention in scholarship on policy advice and expert knowledge. Its role has only grown in importance amid accelerating democratic backsliding and the increased personalisation of politics in many jurisdictions. This article argues that policy scholarship can build on insights from other social science disciplines, which have a long-standing and rich tradition of researching trust, to develop a more purposeful and systematic approach to analysing interpersonal trust and its role in policy making. It sets out a research agenda for studying the phenomena that advances understanding of the informal dimensions of policy making, which have largely remained elusive. entries.title: Policy advisory systems and democratic governance in Italy
entries.abstract: Policy advisory systems (PASs) shape how governments organise and use expertise, yet their implications for democratic governance remain underexplored. This article examines how the governance of PASs influences democratic responsiveness and democratic accountability, asking how different organisational arrangements shape these core democratic dimensions. Focusing on the Italian PAS between 2020 and 2025, the article analyses how organisational analytical capacity mediates the relationship between democracy and technocracy. Drawing on a longitudinal case study of three governments, it discusses the consequences of the features and dynamics of the PAS (such as the creation of new advisory bodies, pluralisation, inclusiveness, adaptability, politicisation and elite circulation) on democratic governance. entries.title: Corruption Perceptions, the Pendleton Act, and Sovereign Borrowing Costs
entries.abstract: ABSTRACT Significant research suggests that systems of bureaucratic patronage tend to promote corruption and reduce the efficient production of publicly provided goods. However, much less work has been done to consider how market actors perceive such selection processes and especially reforms implemented to reduce such corruption. This study rectifies this by evaluating how the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act impacted federal borrowing costs. If patronage resulted in increased corruption and bureaucratic inefficiency, this should be reflected in relatively higher bond yields. If the Pendleton Act was successful in curbing this behavior, then this should be rewarded by market actors in the form of lower borrowing costs. entries.title: “Unseen and unheard”: recognition and its role in shaping administrative burden
entries.abstract: Abstract Administrative burden scholarship has identified psychological costs alongside learning and compliance costs, yet the category remains homogeneous, grouping stigma, diminished autonomy, and stress, without a shared organizing principle. This article advances a mechanism-level account centered on recognition, drawing on a qualitative case study of claiming disability benefits in Israel, based on in-depth interviews with thirty-three individuals (sixteen young adults with diagnosed mental health conditions and seventeen social and outreach workers).
